Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Goal 2 Rules summary 3 Movement of the pieces: 4 Playing online 5 Available variants Goal Move all of your pieces to the Home Row opposite your starting position. Rules summary On their turn, each player can: Roll one of their pieces and place it back where it was Move one of the pieces according to the rules for the face-up side Movement of the pieces: Flame: can move straight or diagonally in all directions Book: can move straight in all directions Swords: can move diagonally in all directions Tree: can move straight forward or backwards, and diagonally forward Ear: cannot move at all! Hat: can move two steps straight then one step on the side, in all directions (like the knight in chess) A piece can jump over an adjacent piece if there is an open space on the other side of the piece being jumped in the direction of the jumping piece's movement. The first time a piece is jumped over during a turn, it has to be rolled. After a jump, all pieces (except for the hat) can go on jumping as long as there is another valid jump available from the landing space. A piece can freely move within its Home Row as long as it did not leave it. After it leaves though, it can't reenter its Home Row. A piece arrived into their destination Home Row cannot move afterwards. Nonetheless, it can always finish a series of jumps before coming to a rest. Playing online Reordering your pieces : before starting to play, each player can reorder their pieces in their Home Row. To accomplish this, you can drag and drop a piece over another to exchange their positions. When you are done, click on the 'I'm finished' link above the play space. When all players are finished reordering, the game starts. Select a piece : click on a piece. Available destinations for this piece (jumps comprised) are then highlighted. Move a piece : click on the destination you want to move to. After a jump, if it is possible to make another jump, corresponding destinations will be highlighted. You can also stop where you are by clicking on the 'I'm finished' link above the play space. Path selection : in order to move to a given destination, the hat can select between two moves. Either two steps forward then one on the side, or one step on the side then two steps forward. Distinct pieces may be rolled by following one path or another. Choosing the movement you want is done by clicking the link '1->2' or the link '2->1' (selected path is then highlighted), then by clicking the link 'I'm finished' above the play space. Available variants Random start : for a more random game, starting pieces are rolled (Ears are rolled again until getting only moving pieces). Rule of Chaos : to encourage more chaos, a player cannot cross the middle of the board with any of their pieces until their starting Home Row has been emptied: all pieces have to be put in play at the same time. Random start & Rule of Chaos : combination of the two previous variants. Have a good game ! But this game seems to introduce randomness for the sake of randomness... which I find to be bad game design.   While the random elements do introduce new decisions and force players to "gamble" with probabilities... they largely mitigate any deep decisions players may make. [Rating: 5/10] Table Gype replaces the fixed movement properties of the pieces in Traverse with a die roll that alters the properties of a piece whenever it is jumped. Four faces of the die call for movements that essentially match the movements of the four kinds of pieces in Traverse. A fifth face directs the piece to move as a knight in chess, and the sixth face requires the piece to remain stationary.  Traverse tempted you to look ahead. [Rating: 5/10] Disappointing.  This is Chinese checkers-like, which was not my favourite game to begin with.  Most pieces can move forwards, so with the 1-in-6 exception of the ear, the type of piece you have is not too relevant.  That makes the die rolling more of an annoyance than an integral part of the game.

[Rating: 5/10] This is wacky abstract strategy that can turn on you at all times. Having the pieces roll into something different when jumped is a great mechanic and the game ends quickly enough so as not to outstay its welcome. I feel it has a similarity to Quorridor, as I prefer it with 4 - the crisscrossing lane to victory always makes for some interesting game play.

[Rating: 5/10] This game is comparable to [gameid=3313] from 1987. In contrast to Traverse, this game seems rather quirky. It is one of the few abstract games in which chance is involved through dice rolls.  Even though the game requires more strategy than one might think at first. Another comment reports the kingmaker problem with more than two players. Like Traverse, this game has received a "Mensa Select" award. The people at Mensa must have had something in mind.
